Photographer Tyler Stalman has once again released his annual iPhone camera review. Here are his thoughts on the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Images, and more.

Stalman takes an in-depth look at the variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro

This year's iPhone 18 Pro brings a number of new features, including a 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapor chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, but the biggest camera upgrade is clearly the variable aperture system.

Other updates this year include Cinematic mode, Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Images, and further refinements to professional controls in the Camera app.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman shared his thoughts on all the new hardware and software camera features on the iPhone 18 Pro. As the review embargo has lifted, reviews from major outlets are rolling out, including ours here at 9to5Mac.

Stalman notes that while he really liked the Cosmic Orange color of last year's iPhone 17 Pro, that color tends to reflect light when shooting through the glass. Therefore, he recommends professional photographers consider Deep Sea Blue or Black, as these colors are less likely to introduce unwanted color casts to photos and videos.

He also notes upfront that this review compares the iPhone 18 Pro camera to the iPhone 15 Pro, and that the review video itself was shot almost entirely on the iPhone 17 Pro.

Speaking to the headline upgrade for the main camera — the new variable aperture — Stalman says the feature is "a huge step in making the iPhone a real camera."

He also points out that the larger f/1.48 aperture lets more light reach the sensor, helping to keep ISO lower in low-light conditions and reducing the number of times Night mode kicks in.

This portion of the review features great photos of the aperture blades opening and closing. Stalman mentions that one unique aspect of Apple's design is that the aperture blades are placed in front of the main lens element, rather than tucked deep within the optics as in traditional camera designs.

Stalman also notes that the 4x zoom on the iPhone 18 Pro (also present on last year's model) is a notable improvement over the 5x zoom on the iPhone 16 Pro, as the focal length of the 5x zoom sometimes feels a touch too tight.

Speaking to features that might have "gone too far," he briefly mentions the new AI editing tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Re-Frame, noting that while they're technically impressive and the results are realistic enough, they alter the image so much that the final product loses the feel of the original.

Speaking to the iPhone 18 Pro's new texture options — Smooth Skin, Glow, and Film — Stalman demonstrates the effect of each option at various intensities from 0 to 100. His conclusion: Smooth Skin effectively reduces skin texture subtly rather than just blurring skin tones; Glow produces a diffused highlight bloom effect reminiscent of professional Black Pro-Mist filters.

He was also impressed by the grain and halation effects of the Film mode, though he wishes Apple would give users more options to control the intensity of the grain.

The review also covers Apple Reference Images, iPhone Cinematic mode (and why Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic video), the new Apple Log 2, and is interspersed with photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.
